analysis.one_liner: Caps out-of-pocket insulin costs at $25 a month and bans insulin deductibles and prior-authorization for insured patients.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or floor action: it was referred to the Senate Health committee, sat there for nearly two years, and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required private health plans, employer plans, and Medicare to cap what patients pay for a month's supply of insulin at $25 — or, for private insurance, 25% of the drug's negotiated price if that is lower. It would have also banned insurers from applying a deductible to insulin and from requiring prior authorization or step therapy before covering it, and it would have cut the Medicare insulin cap from $35 to $25 a month. It never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 8 million Americans who use insulin. Under the bill, they would pay no more than $25 a month out of pocket for covered insulin, would not have to meet their deductible first, and could not be made to jump through prior-authorization or step-therapy hoops to get it. Medicare beneficiaries' cap would drop from $35 to $25 a month [S2, S3].

how_it_helps.text: Caps patient cost-sharing for a month's insulin supply at $25 or 25% of the net negotiated price, whichever is less, and eliminates the deductible and prior-authorization hurdles for those products under private insurance [S2, S3].
Lowers the Medicare Part D insulin cap from $35 to $25 per month for 2024 and 2025 [S2].
Requires at least one insulin of each type and dosage form (vial, pump, inhaler) to be covered, so patients on uncommon forms are not left out [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers sponsoring plans would absorb the difference between current patient cost-sharing and the $25 cap, likely passed into premiums; insulin manufacturers would lose some high-cost-sharing revenue. Patients themselves are not the payers under this bill [S3].

drawbacks.text: The mandate applies only to each plan's selected insulin products — plans can pick which products to cover and can still impose high cost-sharing on insulin outside that selection, and on any insulin from out-of-network providers [S3].
Insurers and employers, not drug makers, bear the cost-sharing mandate: the bill restricts what patients pay without capping what manufacturers charge, so plans' premium costs could rise [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: insulin is a daily, life-or-death drug, and a $25 cap with no deductible would remove a barrier that causes people to ration doses. The cost is borne by employers and private insurers, who would likely absorb it through premiums, and some of the bill's scope (e.g., out-of-network insulin and non-selected products) is left unregulated, which softens its reach. On balance the benefits to the roughly eight million insulin-using Americans are significant and the design is workable; the main weakness is that it was written to die in committee rather than to become law.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred it to its Health committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never voted on it, and the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Josh Hawley introduced S. 146 in the Senate on January 30, 2023 [S1, S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day [S5].
It picked up one Democratic cosponsor out of 48 Senate Democrats [S4].

The only other activity in nearly two years was a Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs hearing in June 2024 at which the bill's subject was discussed; the Health committee never reported the bill, and no floor vote ever occurred [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one who needs insulin is better off; insurers and pharmaceutical manufacturers are spared any new federal requirements, and their pricing and cost-sharing practices continue unchanged.

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 30, 2023; it was read twice and referred to committee [S1, S5].

for.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
for.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 30, 2023 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: A Republican introduced the bill with one Democratic cosponsor; no votes were ever taken, so the record shows no party split on the merits.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer health plans
industries.note: The bill forces plans to cover insulin with no deductible and low, predictable cost-sharing, while letting them choose which products to cover and what manufacturers charge. Their gatekeeping role over insulin access remains intact.

The cost-sharing cap is calculated net of all price concessions 'including... pharmacy benefit management services,' explicitly counting rebates PBMs negotiate — reducing a lever PBM deals have over what patients pay at the counter.

The bill caps what patients pay, not what manufacturers charge, so manufacturers keep their list prices and reimbursement from insurers. They lose the high-cost-sharing customer cost-shifting but keep pricing power.
